That service can be accessed by a Windows app on the studio PC, an iPhone app, a web app, or an Elgato Stream Deck; every device in the room needed to record an episode is fully remote controlled. I have created multiple single-use iOS apps for cataloguing and measuring items and designed and 3D-printed a measurement rig. I have also designed and purchased the items for several dedicated hardware devices, including a device for direct interaction with an agent, and dedicated display devices for the studio. I have created a full-fledged iOS app (designed for the Duo, but it works on regular iPhones) for accessing the various computers I manage; it works across screen sharing, terminals, and KVM switches. It works on Mac, Linux, and Windows. I honestly think it’s the best screen sharing client ever made. I already use it daily. Along the way I created a small harness for my agent such that it not only choreographs subagents, but also farms out work to various computers I own, depending on the load: a Mac for iOS development, a gaming PC for GPU-related work, and a Linux server for everything else. That work is tracked on a custom status board that runs on every TV in my house, as an iOS app, and as a Telegram bot. All of this would have taken teams of people weeks of work, if not months, just a few years ago; I, however, have AI. It only takes an individual. The Deflationary Employee The largest company of the 1950s, as measured by market capitalization, was AT&T; in 1959 it had revenue of $7.54 billion and a market cap of $17.1 billion. It had 729,000 employees. In inflation-adjusted terms that’s revenue of $87.5 billion and a market cap of $198.4 billion; we don’t apply inflation to employees. Or, maybe we do, but in the other direction: what has been striking about the most valuable companies in the world is how their employee numbers have deflated , even as their revenue and market cap have exploded. All dollar numbers in this table are inflation-adjusted to today: Decade Company Year Real revenue Employees Real market cap 1950s AT&T 1959 $87.5B 729,000 $198.4B 1960s AT&T 1969 $147.8B ~1,000,000 $245.6B 1970s IBM 1979 $106.3B 337,119 $174.8B 1980s IBM 1989 $170.6B 383,220 $148.5B 1990s General Electric 1999 $226.6B 340,000 $1.03T 2000s ExxonMobil 2008 $749.5B 104,700 $637.6B 2010s Apple 2018 $355.9B 132,000 $1.00T 2020s Apple 2026 $478.8B 167,000 $5.07T The deflation is even more extreme if you consider two of the seminal AI companies, Nvidia and Anthropic: Decade Company Year Real revenue Employees Real market cap 2020s Nvidia 2026 $361.8B 42,000 $3.99T 2020s Anthropic 2026 $35.3B 5,300 $1.17T This translates into a stunning rise in revenue/employee and market cap/employee — note that this graph is a logarithmic scale: And yet, even this chart, which pegs the market cap/employee of Nvidia at $95 million, doesn’t come close to what the market decided one particular Nvidia employee is worth: As ChatGPT, which helped me make these charts, helpfully noted: Nvidia gained nearly $1 trillion in market capitalization following Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO. That gain alone exceeds the entire inflation-adjusted market capitalization of ExxonMobil in 2008 ($638 billion). It only takes an individual. The Huang Odyssey To describe the two-week odyssey of Nvidia’s then-and-now-CEO Jensen Huang as surreal is an understatement; what you can’t argue, however, is that it was unprecedented: it was only three Thanksgivings ago that Sam Altman was deposed and reinstated as OpenAI CEO over the very same weekend (two Max Verstappen Las Vegas Grand Prix wins, I might note). That said, I didn’t think that this episode would end the same way, and said as much on Sharp Tech : whereas Altman was taken out by a somewhat ham-fisted internal coup and restored through pressure from the private company’s investors and employees, Huang appeared to be targeted by a much more systemic campaign by powerful actors leveraging the media and barely disguised insinuations of malfeasance to leave the Nvidia board with no choice but to act. And, to be sure, Huang gave his enemies plenty of ammunition; I’ve invoked the phrase “Show me the man and I’ll show you the crime” over the past few weeks, but it’s worth acknowledging that Huang basically asked his critics, “Which one?”, at least as far as his sexual proclivities were concerned. At the same time, it sure seemed like no one cared about Huang’s affairs, including those with subordinates; the real crime appeared to be Huang’s resolute advocacy for selling chips to China, his refusal to do any more than the bare minimum to abide by export control rules, and, his most ardent critics allege, turning a blind eye towards actual smuggling. I’m not here, today at least, to litigate these accusations; I covered much of it in last week’s Article Obituaries (alternate title for today: Resurrections ).
